title: Finding Duplicate Records Across Columns
description: Find all **duplicate email addresses** in the customers table (emails that appear more than once). Show the email, how many times it appears, and all the customer IDs that share that email.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id INT, name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(200), phone VARCHAR(20)); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Alice Smith','alice@email.com','555-1234'),(2,'Alice S.','alice@email.com','555-5678'),(3,'Bob Jones','bob@email.com','555-2345'),(4,'Carol White','carol@email.com','555-3456'),(5,'Carol W.','carol@email.com','555-7890'),(6,'Dave Brown','dave@email.com','555-4567'),(7,'Eve Davis','eve@email.com','555-5678'),(8,'Bob J.','bob@email.com','555-9012');
solution_sql: SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS occurrence_count, STRING_AGG(customer_id::TEXT, ', ' ORDER BY customer_id) AS customer_ids FROM customers GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY occurrence_count DESC, email

test_cases.description: 3 duplicate emails: alice@email.com(2), bob@email.com(2), carol@email.com(2). dave@email.com and eve@email.com are unique.

hints: GROUP BY email and use HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to keep only emails that appear more than once.
Use STRING_AGG(customer_id::TEXT, ', ' ORDER BY customer_id) to list all customer IDs sharing the duplicate email as a comma-separated string.
explanation: Grouping by email and filtering with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 identifies duplicates. alice@email.com appears for customer IDs 1 and 2. bob@email.com appears for IDs 3 and 8. carol@email.com appears for IDs 4 and 5. dave@email.com and eve@email.com appear only once each — excluded. STRING_AGG lists the affected customer IDs for deduplication review.
